documentation.range: Atlantic Bonito live along the tropical and temperate coasts of both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of Mexico and the Mediterranean and Black seas (Collette and Chao 1975). In the western Atlantic, they have been found as far north as the outer coast of Nova Scotia, but their usual northern limit is Cape Ann, Massachusetts. Atlantic Bonito are uncommon around southern Florida, present in the northern Gulf of Mexico, but apparently absent from most of the Caribbean Sea. They occur in Colombia and Venezuela and are much more common south of the Amazon River to northern Argentina. In the eastern Atlantic, they have been caught near Oslo, Norway and in Irish waters south through the Gulf of Guinea to Port Elizabeth, South Africa as well as in the Mediterranean and Black seas (Collette and Graves,2019).
documentation.population:
There are significant genetic differences between Mediterranean and northwest Atlantic populations of Atlantic Bonito (Viñas et al. 2004, 2010). There are also genetic differences between populations in the Mediterranean with the Black and Marmara Sea populations comprising one genetic unit, the Aegean and Mediterranean coast of Turkey populations a second unit, and the Adriatic Sea population genetically different from those two units (Turan 2015, Turan et al. 2016). In the western Atlantic, there are some morphometric and meristic differences between populations of Atlantic Bonito in the western North Atlantic and those off the coast of Argentina which have fewer vertebrae, gill rakers, and fin rays (Collette and Chao 1975, Hansen 1988a).

Global FAO statistics show that landings have fluctuated with no apparent increasing or decreasing trends between  20,146 and 55, 967 mt from 2009 to 2018 (FAO 2020). This pattern extends as far back as the 1950s, with a minimum of 14842 mt in 1950 and a maximum of 83059 mt in 2005 (FAO 2021). Turkey and Morocco are among the nations with the highest reported landings.

In Mexico, catches reported to ICCAT around the years 2000-2013 are stable and average approximately 1000-1100 metric tons (ICCAT database); from 2008 to 2018 landings varied from 1,113 to 3,685 metric tons. Catches in the U.S. are very low, with only significant recorded catches in recreational fisheries. For example, a small regional fishery in the Chesapeake Bay fluctuated from a few pounts to 160,000 pounds annually (Mansueti 1962). It is common in the Gulf of Mexico.
documentation.habitats:
Atlantic Bonito are a small epipelagic species that occurs in schools. They sometimes enter estuaries and have a depth range of 0-200 m. They are migratory in the eastern Mediterranean Sea with schools spending the summers in the Black Sea and winters in the Sea of Marmara and the Augean Sea. They can adapt to gradual but not sudden changes in the environment and may occur in water temperatures between 12 and 27°C and salinities between 14 and 39 entering estuaries such as Miramichi and the Gulf of St. Lawrence.  The Argentine bonito fleet caught Atlantic Bonito by itself the most often, with Skipjack Tuna the next most often, and with Little Tunny the next most often (Hansen 1988b).

Adult Atlantic Bonito prey primari1y on small schooling fishes such as sardines, anchovies, and mackerel and also on squids, the choice of species depending on the locality. In the Gulf of Mexico, they feed on anchovies and other fishes, squids, and shrimps (Boschung, 1966). They can swallow relatively large prey, and both juveniles and adults are known to be cannibalistic. In the southern Tyrrhenian Sea, the diet is largely herring-like fishes, especially sardines and anchovies (Campo et al. 2006). Smaller individuals prefer anchovies and switch to sardines as they increase in size. The diet is similar in the northeast Aegean Sea (Fletcher et al. 2013) with the addition of picarel porgies (Centracanthidae).During migration to the Black Sea, many individuals had empty stomachs but those that had fed consumed small pelagic fishes, especially the anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus which had an Index of Relative Importance of 94% (Genç et al. 2019). Two other major prey items were Trachurus mediterraneus and Sprattus sprattus.

Atlantic Bonito are multiple spawners with asynchronous oocyte development that releases eggs multiple times throughout the spawning season (Rey et al. 1984, Macias et al. 2005). They are migratory (Sabates and Recasens 2001) and both spawning season and size of maturity varies between populations. Two main spawning areas have been defined both geographically and temporally within the Mediterranean (Vinas et al. 2004). The first area is in the western Mediterranean including the Alboran Sea, waters south of the Balearic Islands and waters off the Algerian coast where spawning occurs during early summer. The second area is at the eastern end of the Mediterranean and includes the coastal waters of the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea with spawning occurring between May and August with a maximum in June and July. In most parts of the Mediterranean, they spawn between May and July but off Algeria, spawning extends from March to May. In the eastern Atlantic, spawning occurs from December to June, including peaks in January and April, off Dakar, and from June to July in Moroccan waters. In the northwestern Atlantic, bonitos spawn in June and July. Atlantic Bonito mature in their first year (Rey et al. 1984). Length at first maturity is 35.8-39.5 cm in males and 40.5-42.5 cm in females (Kahraman et al. 2014).

The maximum reported size of Atlantic Bonito in the Black Sea is 85 cm FL and 5 kg (Ates et al. 2008). In the western Atlantic, the largest fish measured 91.4 cm FL and weighed 5.4 kg. They are common to 50 cm FL and about 2 kg.  Atlantic Bonito reach at least 4 years of age in the Mediterranean. Several studies report estimated sizes at age for Atlantic Bonito in the Mediterranean and Gulf of Guinea: age 0: 35-37 cm; 1: 38-52 cm; 2: 45-57 cm; 3: 58-65 cm; and 4: 64-71 cm. Growth curves indicate Atlantic Bonito in Argentina may reach 8 years with mean lengths at age 1: 42 cm; 2: 50 cm, 3: 54 cm; 4:58 cm; 5:62 cm; 6: 69 cm; and 8:72 cm (Hansen 1989; Collette and Graves, 2019). There were no significant differences between sexes in fork length in a sample of 665 Atlantic Bonito from the Adriatic Sea (Franičevič et al. 2005) or a sample of 212 from the Black Sea (Kahraman et al. 2014).

The all-tackle game fish record is of an 8.3 kg (18 lb, 4 oz) fish caught off Faial Island in the Azores in 1953 (IGFA 2021).
documentation.threats:
There are fisheries of various sizes throughout most of the range of Atlantic Bonito. It is one of the most important species in the Black Sea ecosystem (Genç et al., 2019) and is the most important species among Black Sea fishes in terms of commercial value (Zengin and Cemal Dinçer, 2006). It is also important in the Mediterranean (Demir 1963) and in Argentina (Hansen 1987). In the period from 1978 to 1981, 11 countries reported catches of S. sarda from Fishing Area 37, steadily increasing from 9,400 to about 29,400 metric tons per year (FAO, 1983). Fishing in the Black Sea peaks between May and October, while in the Mediterranean it may vary from area to area or even extend throughout the year. In Argentina, the fishing season is in the southern summer with landings beginning in the last week of January, increasing up to March, and then decreasing sharply (Hansen 1987).The yearly world catch reported for the species in the above period trended upwards from 14,892 to 41,385 metric tons (FAO, 1983). Fishing in the eastern tropical Atlantic takes place between October and May, while it extends throughout the year off Morocco. In the Bay of Biscay, the season is much shorter, from mid-April to mid-May; however, Spanish vessels may extend their operation through November. Peak fishing of the Spanish fleet all around the peninsula is in late spring and in fall. In the western Atlantic (Gulf of Maine), Atlantic bonito is taken between June and October (Collette and Graves, 2019).

The total catch for this species in 1999 as reported to FAO was 37 240 t. The countries with the largest catches were Turkey (17 900 t) and Mexico (2 314 t) (FAO 2021).
documentation.measures: The original global assessment of Sarda sarda in 2011 was Least Concern (Collette et al. 2011).After the 2011 global assessment, regional assessments of Least Concern were made for the populations in the Mediterranean in 2011 and the Gulf of Mexico in 2015. The minimum landing size for Atlantic Bonito in Turkey is 25 cm (Ateș et al. 2008, Cengiz 2013). To prevent catch of sexually immature age groups O and 1, current bonito fishing practices should be regulated by applying fishing quotas per boat in the Black Sea fishery (Zegin et al. 2005). Most fish landed in Turkey and Morocco are below mature size, indicating that the stock may not be able to renew or sustain itself long-term (Oray et al. 2004, Ateș et al. 2008, Cengiz 2013, Baibbat et al. 2019). The fishing pressure in the northeastern part of the Atlantic exceeds the optimum which indicates stock overfishing is taking place (Petukhova 2020).
documentation.use_trade: This species is an important food fish, targeted by fisheries throughout its range. It is particularly important in the Mediterranean and Black seas and off Argentina where it is taken by trap net, ring net, gillnet, trammel net, purse seine, beach seine, and hook and line (Demir 1963). It is also taken as bycatch in fisheries targeting mackerel with beach seines and gillnets (SAGARPA 2012).
documentation.rationale: This is a very widespread species that is fairly fast growing and abundant in many areas. It has been caught in both commercial and recreational fisheries for a long period of time with no evident overall or significant population declines. Therefore, this species is listed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: There is some genetic differentiation between samples from the Atlantic and those from the Mediterranean, but not at the species level (Vinas et al. 2010).
